items.prompt: What is 'BDD (behavior-driven development)'?
choices: Writing tests that describe what a system does, from the outside, in terms of its actual observable behavior
A development process where designers write all the tests instead of engineers
Writing tests only after a feature has been in production for at least a month
A testing framework that requires no assertions at all
items.explanation: BDD is specifically about testing observable behavior from the outside, not implementation details, and not a specific team-role or timing rule.
items.reference:
BDD
👁️ Describes observable behavior
🚫 Not internal implementation
Why: this is what makes BDD tests survive internal refactors.

Neither style has anything to do with BDD
items.explanation: Tests against the public methods describe observable behavior, exactly what BDD is about — the internal-state assertions are the opposite approach.
items.reference:
BDD
👁️ Describes observable behavior
🚫 Not internal implementation
Why: this is what makes BDD tests survive internal refactors.

items.prompt: What is a class's 'public interface'?

Any method that happens to be called 'public' in its name

items.explanation: The public interface is the set of methods and behaviors external code actually relies on — the real contract, regardless of naming conventions or comments.
items.reference:
Public interface
📞 What external code actually calls
🤝 The real contract
Why: only this part of a class is safe to test against long-term.

items.prompt: What is an 'implementation detail'?

A comment describing what a function does
A bug that has not yet been discovered

🔧 Free to change internally
✅ As long as behavior stays the same

items.prompt: What does the 'Given-When-Then' structure describe?

⚡ When: action
👁️ Then: observable outcome
